paper.title: On Additional Constrains in Lossless Compression of Text Files
paper.abstract: Coding algorithms are generally aimed at minimizing the output code length encoding speed once the code has been designed. Moreover, most codes use a binary alphabet. This paper examines other issues related to coding, such as additional constraints imposed on the channel. Code generation will be considered where there is a limit on code words. Limits the application of such systems is a practical example of data compression where fast decoding is essential. When all code words correspond to a single word in memory (usually 32 bits, but there are situations that take 64-bit) can be used canonical decoding. If the deadline cannot be guaranteed, however, required the use of slower decoding methods. This paper also deals with the alphabetic code generation, where lexicographic arrangement of words by their code symbols must correspond to the original order in which the symbols were taken coding system. When an alphabetic code is used to compress a database that can be sorted in the same, order they would have had if the database records were first decompressed and then sorted. It also corresponds to alphabetic code trees binary search trees, which have applications in a wide variety of search problems. Assumption that the symbols are sorted by probability is not suitable for this scenario. The problem of finding codes for non-binary alphabets channel will be examined in detail. The subsequent experimental results cover the problem of alphabetic coding and of limited length coding.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Implementation and empirical evaluation of two existing constrained prefix-coding methods, alphabetic coding (Hu-Tucker with Knuth's priority-queue implementation) and length-limited coding by the reverse package-merge algorithm of Turpin and Moffat, on the Calgary and Canterbury corpora and a few Romanian text files, with a short discussion of unequal-cost channel alphabets (Morse code).
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** The paper proposes no algorithm of its own. It describes published algorithms in prose, reports that they were implemented in an application with a graphical interface, and compares compression rate and time against WinRAR and an arithmetic coder. This is a performance comparison of existing algorithms, the Level 2 example in the specification.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0 (with constraints: 0)
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 0 (one inline complexity remark, O(n^2) for Hu-Tucker, and an inline statement of the alphabetic ordering constraint whose relation symbols were lost in text extraction)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate. There is no formal apparatus to be disproportionate. The paper errs the other way: the algorithms are described so loosely that a reader could not implement them from the text (Section 4, on the limited-length algorithm, is two sentences long), and the unequal-cost channel problem that the abstract says "will be examined in detail" receives neither a formulation nor an experiment.

### Issues
None identified under the necessity test.

---

## Citation Analysis

Single-author paper. 17 of the 26 references are to the author's own work ([2], [8], [10], [13]-[26]), a self-citation ratio of 65%, more than twice the 30% threshold. All of them are on lossless compression. The text-compression items (transforms, Huffman implementations, the author's compression books) are related; the image-compression tools ([8], [18], [22]) and the two teaching-tool papers from a seminar on quality management in higher education ([23], [24]) are marginal, with estimated similarity 0.3-0.5, but none falls below 0.3, so IRRELEVANT_SELF_CITATION is not raised.

Two features aggravate the ratio. First, the reference list is padded: the body cites only [5], [11] and [12], so none of the 17 self-citations supports any statement in the paper. Second, the list contains duplicates: [10] and [21] are the same ISSCS 2009 paper, [2] and [14] are the same 2003 MatrixRom book under slightly different titles, and [25] and [26] are the same title published in two venues. Historical and technical claims in Sections 1-3 (Hu and Tucker 1971, Knuth's improvement, Morse 1835, a zero bit costing 10% more energy) carry no citation.

---

## Structural Analysis

The experimental evidence is thin and partly inconsistent. Results are given only as bar charts (Figs. 1-5) with no numeric table; the only table lists five Romanian files under a leftover template caption ("Type Sizes for Camera-Ready Papers"), and the corpus files actually used are never listed. The paragraph describing Fig. 1 (alphabetic coding) is repeated almost verbatim for Fig. 2 (limited-length coding), including the sentence that "imposing an upper limit on the words, has led to compression rates of about 1.4÷1.5", so the alphabetic-coding figure is described in terms of the length limit. Compression rate is defined as "the output file size divided by the size of the input file", yet a higher rate is treated as better and WinRAR is said to give "a compression rate of 54 for the file in Excel", which fits only the inverse definition. The conclusion that limited-length coding "guarantees a good to very good compression of a variety of files" sits uneasily with Section 5.C, which reports it is "surpassed by other methods of compression in all cases". The coding algorithm is twice called an "encryption" algorithm. Estimated CER about 0.4: weak, above the 0.33 threshold.

Limitations: no dedicated section; inline acknowledgment that timing depends on the workstation used and that limited-length coding is outperformed by WinRAR and arithmetic coding.

Artifacts: an "application accompanying this paper" is mentioned, with no link or availability statement. The Calgary and Canterbury corpora on which most results rest are public and linked in [11] and [12]; the Romanian test files are not. Category: data.

---

## Conclusion

A comparison of existing constrained-coding algorithms with no formalism problem, disqualified on citation conduct: 65% of the reference list is the author's own work, none of it cited in the text, and some of it duplicated. EXCESSIVE_SELF_CITATION disqualifies at any concept level. Independently of the flag, the reporting is weak: results exist only as charts, paragraphs are duplicated across figures, the metric is defined inconsistently with the values reported, and the conclusions overstate the method.

paper.title: P-Type Doping of 4H-SiC for Integrated Bipolar and Unipolar Devices
paper.abstract: P-type 4H-SiC layers formed by ion implantation need high temperature processes, which generate surface roughness, losing and incomplete activation of dopants. Due to dopant redistribution and channeling effect, it is difficult to predict the depth of the formed junctions. Vapor-Liquid-Solid (VLS) selective epitaxy is an alternative method to obtain locally highly doped p-type layers in the 10^20 cm^-3 range or more. The depth of this p-type layers or regions is accurately controlled by the initial Reactive-Ion-Etching (RIE) of the SiC. Lateral Junction Field Effect Transistor (JFET) devices are fabricated by integrating p-type layers created by Al ion implantation or VLS growth. The p-type VLS layers improve the access resistances on the electrodes of the fabricated devices.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Overview comparing two ways of forming local p-type regions in 4H-SiC, aluminium ion implantation with high-temperature annealing (with graphite-cap surface protection) and Vapor-Liquid-Solid selective epitaxy, and their use in monolithically integrated lateral JFETs. The evidence is sheet-resistance, AFM, SIMS, RBS/C, TLM and I-V measurements, much of it from the group's earlier publications.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** An experimental comparison of process technologies. There is no model, algorithm, or proof; the contribution is empirical. (Semiconductor process work, outside computer science proper.)

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0 (with constraints: 0)
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 0 (numerical values and units only)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate. The paper argues entirely from measurement and cited process literature, which is the appropriate register for its subject.

### Issues
None identified.

---

## Citation Analysis

11 of the 19 references ([4], [5], [10], [11], [13]-[19]) include at least one of the ten authors; M. Lazar is on ten of them. SCR = 57.9%. Every self-citation is topically close (similarity well above 0.5): implantation annealing, dopant loss and redistribution, VLS growth, ohmic contacts on VLS layers, and the two JFET batches the paper reports. The self-citations do real work, pointing to process details and prior measurements (Fig. 1 is taken from [4]; the VLS process "is detailed in [13]"; the JFET batches are "detailed in [17]" and "[18]"). The paper is in effect a synthesis of the group's own programme, which explains the ratio, but the 30% condition for EXCESSIVE_SELF_CITATION is met regardless. No irrelevant self-citation and no ring pattern. Reference [19] is dated 2016 in a 2015 issue, presumably in press. External work is cited for annealing ranges, alternative capping methods and the Monte-Carlo implantation code [12].

---

## Structural Analysis

Claims are generally backed by figures or citations: the sheet-resistance trends with annealing temperature and time, the roughness values (0.31, 0.46 and 1.49 nm), the specific contact resistance of 1.3×10^-6 Ω·cm², and the more-than-tenfold increase in P-JFET drain current with VLS source and drain (Fig. 14). The paper anticipates an apparent contradiction (dopant loss versus falling sheet resistance) and resolves it by pointing to the capped samples. Weaknesses: a good part of the evidence is reproduced from earlier publications rather than new; sample counts, repeat measurements and the device dimensions behind the JFET comparison are not given. Estimated CER above 1.0.

Limitations are acknowledged inline and plainly: VLS growth "is still an immature technological process", reliable P/N junctions by VLS seem "yet premature", interface defects explain the high gate-source leakage of the VLS JFETs, and the current plateau in Fig. 11 is identified as a measurement artifact of the source-measure unit.

Artifacts: no measurement data or other material is released or offered; the work is experimental fabrication. Category: none.

---

## Conclusion

A well-evidenced device-technology overview with no formalism and candid limitations. It is disqualified on a mechanical criterion: 58% of the references are the authors' own, although every one of them is topically relevant and the ratio follows from the paper's character as a summary of the group's line of work.

paper.title: On the Necessary Verification of Fabrication Stages for SOI CMOS Humidity Sensors
paper.abstract: A humidity sensor, which is part of an air quality sensor system, based on MWCNTs/MMA composite doped with KOH has been studied. A standard SOI CMOS process, with only one post-processing step for the membrane etching, was used to fabricate the sensor presented. In order to have a homogeneous distribution of the CNTs in the solution, the tip sonication method was employed. The current voltage and resistance voltage characteristics have been investigated, for different temperatures. Within the sensing layer of the proposed humidity sensor, the parabolic dependence of the resistance with the voltage applied has been proven for positive voltage values. The corresponding first and second order coefficients have been extracted.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

(3) being dimensionally confused; Eqs. (4)-(5), (7)-(8) and (11) dress a standard quadratic TCR model and a second-order polynomial fit in an infinite Taylor series with an ill-formed remainder condition, and the derivative definitions of the coefficients are never evaluated.

verdict.summary: Preliminary SOI CMOS humidity-sensor fabrication report, disqualified at Level 2 for formalism theater (unused textbook humidity definitions and a Taylor-series derivation of a quadratic fit); the claim that a parabolic R-V dependence is proven is weakly supported and humidity testing is deferred to future work.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Fabrication of a resistive humidity sensor by depositing a MWCNT/MMA composite doped with KOH (recipe adapted from Su and Wang [2]) on the interdigitated electrodes of SOI CMOS micro-hotplate chips, with I-V and R-V measurements at six heater-set temperatures and a qualitative response to humidity.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** The paper applies a published sensing-material recipe to a standard CMOS platform and characterises it with basic curve fitting. No new model or method is proposed; the work is close to a prototype description (Level 1), and Level 2 is the upper reading.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 3 (absolute, relative and saturation humidity, Eqs. 1-3, in a subsection titled "Basic definitions"; dew point and frost point are defined in prose)
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 12

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 6
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0.4x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate by count, but several elements fail the Necessity Test, and at Level 2 a single failure triggers FORMALISM_THEATER.

### Issues
- Eqs. (1) and (3), absolute humidity m_w/v and saturation humidity m_ws/v × 100, are never used again; no humidity quantity is measured or computed anywhere in the paper beyond "~98% relative humidity" from a breath on the chip. Eq. (3) multiplies a mass-per-volume ratio by 100 as if it were a percentage. The dew-point and frost-point paragraphs are equally unused. The whole subsection could be replaced by a citation.
- Eqs. (4)-(5) write out the full Taylor series of R(T), with an infinite remainder sum and the ill-formed condition "O[((T − T0)n≥3)] → 0", and Eqs. (7)-(8) define α_T and β_T as normalised derivatives, only to arrive at the standard quadratic temperature-coefficient model of Eq. (6). The derivatives are never evaluated: α_T = 2.05×10^-3 K^-1 and β_T = 3×10^-7 K^-2 are simply stated. Eqs. (11)-(12) repeat the exercise for R(V) to justify fitting a second-order polynomial. "We fit R(T) and R(V) with second-order polynomials" says the same thing.
- Functional elements: Eq. (6) and its inversion, Eq. (10), are used to infer the six sensing-layer temperatures from ΔR/R0, and the form of Eq. (12) is what Table 2 fits. These pass the test.
- Minor: "(where 1 L = 1 ltr = 10^-3 m^3, in SI base units)".

DECORATIVE_DEFINITIONS is not raised: the definitions are standard physical quantities rather than "Definition N" blocks for data structures, and the problem is already captured by FORMALISM_THEATER.

---

## Citation Analysis

One self-citation out of 21 references ([18], the authors' CAS 2015 conference paper, whose title contains this paper's title): SCR 4.8%, relevant. The present paper appears to be an extended version of [18]; the overlap is signalled only by the citation. The citation numbering in the text appears shifted by one: the verification of fabrication stages is said to have been "performed by the authors previously in [17]", but [17] is the Farahani et al. review and the authors' own paper is [18]; conversely, the textbook definition of humidity is attributed to [18], where the review [17] would be the plausible source. The rest of the list is appropriate humidity-sensor literature.

---

## Structural Analysis

The abstract states that the parabolic dependence of resistance on voltage "has been proven". The fits in Table 2 do not bear that weight: the coefficients change sign and order of magnitude from one temperature to the next (α_v ranges from −11291 to 25974), σ² falls to 0.896 and 0.838 at the two highest temperatures, one point was removed "by a statistical exclusion criterion" that is not described, and no physical interpretation of the coefficients is offered. The humidity response (Figs. 7-8) is qualitative, produced by blowing on the chip ("every time there was a blow on the chip ∼98% relative humidity was applied"), with no reference hygrometer, calibration, or sensitivity, response-time or hysteresis figures, although the introduction sets an accuracy target of ±2% of full scale. The CNT amount "is not fixed", and the text refers to "Figs. 4-5" for graphs that are Figs. 5-6. Estimated CER about 0.6: the descriptive claims are backed by figures, the "proven" claim is not.

Limitations are conceded inline: "Further measurements will prove if it depends on the relative or absolute humidity" and "Our immediate goal is to perform humidity tests on our sensors, for which we will be using a special chamber", which together acknowledge that proper humidity testing has not yet been done.

Artifacts: no data or other material released or offered. Category: none.

---

## Conclusion

A preliminary fabrication report for a CNT-composite humidity sensor whose humidity characterisation has not yet been carried out. At Level 2 it is disqualified by FORMALISM_THEATER: textbook humidity definitions that are never used and a Taylor-series derivation dressing up a quadratic fit. The quadratic temperature-coefficient model actually used to infer temperature is legitimate. The evidence for the headline claim is weak.

paper.title: Low-Voltage Controlled Floating Buck Converter with Imbalanced Stacked MOSFETs Switch (ISMS) for High LED Driving Capability
paper.abstract: This paper presents a cost effective technique for extending LED driving capability of floating buck converters, using an imbalanced stacked MOSFETs switch (ISMS). The ISMS is comprised of a low-voltage transistor and a power MOSFET, biased at a constant voltage, and can be driven by low output capability control blocks. Unlike prior-art, the proposed ISMS does not rely on synchronous switching and identical devices. The overall turn ON/OFF times impact on the converter’s switching frequency is investigated. The proposed technique is validated by implementation in floating buck converters with two high performing control circuits. Hence, a critical conduction mode control block and a variable OFF time controller, fabricated in 40 V and 5 V CMOS technologies, respectively, are used for driving the converter. Measurements are performed for a wide range of LED strings (6-48) and up to 250 V input voltage. Efficiency results reveal a peak value of 97% and switching frequencies between 25 KHz and 170 KHz. Converters with ISMS are experimentally proven to drive up to eight times more LEDs than their regular versions, with higher efficiencies.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

verdict.summary: Sound applied power-electronics paper with proportionate switching-time analysis, low and relevant self-citation, and well-documented measurements; minor overstatement of headline gains and no released artifacts.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** A circuit technique for extending the LED-string length of floating buck converters: a low-voltage MOSFET, switched by a low-voltage controller, stacked under a high-voltage power MOSFET held at a constant gate bias (the imbalanced stacked MOSFETs switch, ISMS). The paper analyses the switching sequence and validates the technique experimentally with two controllers, a commercial critical-conduction-mode driver and the authors' earlier variable OFF-time controller.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** A known topology family (stacked switches, cascode, ESBT) adapted to a new configuration and validated by measurement; the switching-time analysis uses standard textbook expressions [25]. There is no new algorithm, model with proofs, or theoretical result. A case could be made for Level 3 as design novelty; the specification's default is the lower level.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0 (with constraints: 0)
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 8 (turn-ON and turn-OFF times as sums of RC gate-charging intervals and Miller-plateau intervals)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate. The equations are the ordinary circuit analysis a designer needs: they show that SW2's intervals (t2, t3) dominate the transition times and motivate the choice of V_GG and of low-capacitance devices, which is how the paper uses them. They pass the Necessity Test. The analysis is not compared numerically with the measured 120 ns and 350 ns transition times, only described as "consistent with" them, and the definition of τ_2,OFF after Eq. (8) is typographically garbled.

### Issues
None identified.

---

## Citation Analysis

Two self-citations out of 35 references ([18] and [19], the variable OFF-time controller by Anghel, Pristavu and Brezeanu, with A. Vasilica on [19], a name matching the first author's e-mail address): SCR 5.7%. Both are directly relevant; the controller of [19] is one of the two test vehicles. Three datasheets ([16], [30], [31]) come from ON Semiconductor, the employer of two authors; they document components actually used and are not author self-citations. The reference list leans on patents and datasheets, which is normal for power-IC practice. Reference [35] carries a stray "[34]" in its title.

---

## Structural Analysis

Claims rest on measurement: efficiency and switching-frequency maps over input voltage and LED count (Figs. 8, 9, 11, 12), oscilloscope waveforms with measured switching times (Fig. 10), a PSpice check of the modified zero-current detection (Fig. 7), and two comparison tables. A few headline figures run ahead of the data: the abstract's "up to eight times more LEDs" against 48 versus 8 (6×) and 30 versus 4 (7.5×) in Table 1; "up to 250 V" in the abstract and text against "up to 240 V" in Table 1; the "higher efficiencies" claim compares against baseline maxima (94% and 91%) whose origin, measured or datasheet, is not stated. Table 2 sets a DC-input floating buck beside AC/DC flyback and PFC converters at different output currents, so "comparable or superior" is loose. Fig. 12 is captioned as efficiency while showing switching frequency. No repeat measurements or uncertainty are reported. Estimated CER at or above 1.0.

Limitations are acknowledged inline: increased ON resistance, transition times "slightly higher than state-of-the-art stacked topologies", lower LED current and output power than the compared designs, and the need for an external supply in the CrM version.

Artifacts: no schematic files, board design, or measurement data are released or offered; the circuits are described in figures, and description is not availability. Category: none.

---

## Conclusion

A sound applied circuit paper: proportionate and functional analysis, low and relevant self-citation, and well-documented measurements on two controller architectures. The weaknesses are a modest overstatement of headline numbers, a loose state-of-the-art comparison, and no released artifacts.
